tip: 'Dua-duanya' = both of them: 'dua-duanya suka pedas' = they both like spicy food.
'Tempat' + clause = where: 'desa tempat saya lahir' = the village where I was born.
Indonesian pairs 'different' with 'with', not 'from': 'berbeda dengan iklim di Jakarta'. 'Berbeda dari' isn't wrong, but 'dengan' is what you'll usually hear.
'Muda' usually means young, but for fruit it means unripe: 'mangga muda' = unripe mango.
'Beda' is the everyday short form of 'berbeda': 'beda jauh' = very different.
'Kalah jauh' = far behind (literally loses by far): 'kameranya kalah jauh' = its camera is far worse.
'Seperti kapal pecah' (like a wrecked ship) is the classic image for a hopelessly messy room.
Adding '-nya' makes hot into the heat: 'panas' = hot, 'panasnya' = the heat.
'Kayak' = colloquial 'seperti' (like); you hear it everywhere: 'kayak mimpi' = like a dream.
'Pahitnya kayak obat' sounds like family chat – 'kayak' lives in relaxed speech. The moment you write anything formal (an email, a report), it becomes 'seperti'.
'Lengket seperti perangko' – stuck like a stamp – is the set image for two people who are never apart. 'Lengket' alone is the sticky feel of rice or glue.
'Paling' + 'yang pernah' = the most ... ever: 'paling enak yang pernah saya coba' = tastiest I ever tried.
'Adalah' links two nouns (A is B); it doesn't go before an adjective.
'Paling ... dari semua' = the most ... of all: 'paling empuk dari semua kasur' = softest of all the mattresses.
'Paling' also works with time words: 'bangun paling pagi' = up the earliest.
'Ter-' + adjective can replace 'paling': 'termurah' = 'paling murah' = the cheapest.
'Pun' after a noun = even: 'turis pun' = even tourists.
'Ternyata' = it turns out: 'saya kira mahal, ternyata murah' = I thought it was expensive, turns out it's cheap.
'Ter-' marks what happens with nobody intending it: 'tertinggal' = got left behind by accident. The package 'ternyata tertinggal' – it turned out left behind, no one chose that.
'Padahal' = even though / when in fact, for surprising contrast: 'padahal panas' = even though it's hot.
'Justru' = actually / on the contrary, flips an expectation: 'justru dia tertawa' = on the contrary, he laughed.
Doubling a time word = really early/late: 'pagi-pagi' = early in the morning.
'Sejak' = since a starting point: 'sejak tahun lalu' = since last year. The verb itself does not change.
'Terus' after a verb = keeps on: 'hujan turun terus' = it keeps raining.
'Sejak' also takes an event: 'sejak lulus' = since graduating, 'sejak menikah' = since getting married.
'Sejak' marks a running start point: 'sudah buka sejak jam enam' = open since six. Daily hours normally use 'mulai'.
'Selama' + time = during/for: 'selama liburan' = during the holiday, 'selama dua jam' = for two hours.
'Selama' + clause = while/as long as: 'selama tangannya belum sembuh' = while his hand isn't healed yet.
Everyday speech puts the lost item in charge: 'kunci gudang itu belum ketemu' = the warehouse key hasn't turned up. 'Ketemu' is casual – formal writing uses 'ditemukan'.
'Baru saja' + verb = just did: 'baru saja tiba' = just arrived.
